vignette:
He is 62 now, a married African man who has spent most of his adult life working as a bomb disposal technician, the kind of person others describe as steady under pressure. For years, his job has trained him to trust procedure over panic: assess, isolate, contain, disarm. He says that before the incident, he believed that if a man stayed disciplined enough, he could outthink danger. The work was risky, yes, but it was risk he understood. He knew explosives had rules. What happened to him did not feel like it followed rules at all.

The exposure happens during what is supposed to be a controlled response. He and his team are called to inspect a suspicious device found near a storage area on an industrial site. At first, the scene appears familiar-cordon tape, radios crackling, technicians speaking in clipped phrases-but once the casing is disturbed, something ruptures inside. He remembers a sudden hiss, then a strange sweet-metallic smell that cuts through the air before anyone can step back. He does not see flames or shrapnel. Instead, he feels his eyes burning, his throat closing, and a terrifying confusion as his body seems to betray him all at once. He begins coughing so hard he cannot speak. His chest tightens. Tears stream from his eyes, and his skin prickles as if covered with ants. Around him, men are shouting instructions through masks, but the sound becomes distant, warped. He is certain, in those moments, that he is dying from something invisible.

At the hospital, he stays alert in the rigid, overcontrolled way he knows from field operations, but inside he is shaken. He keeps replaying the delay between the hiss and the first burn in his lungs. That gap unsettles him most. An explosion is immediate, but this comes like a hidden invasion. Even after he is medically stabilized, he cannot stop scanning his body for signs that something toxic is still moving through him. A tickle in his throat becomes proof of permanent damage. A headache feels ominous. He wakes at night convinced he can smell that same chemical odor in the bedroom, and he sits upright, breathing through his mouth so he will not inhale more of it. His wife turns on the light and tells him there is nothing there, but by then his heart is pounding and his undershirt is wet with sweat.

When he returns home, he expects recovery to be a matter of toughness. Instead, ordinary things begin to ambush him. Cleaning products in the supermarket aisle make him abandon the cart and wait outside. Fuel fumes at a petrol station leave him dizzy and irritable for the rest of the day. If he hears a pressurized spray can release with a sharp hiss, his whole body locks before he understands why. He grows ashamed of how quickly fear overtakes him. At work, he still knows every protocol, but he no longer trusts his senses. He checks seals and containment equipment repeatedly, then checks them again. Colleagues notice he has become slower, less willing to enter uncertain environments without exhaustive reassurance. He tells them age has made him more cautious. Privately, he worries he has become dangerous to the team because his mind sometimes blanks at the wrong moment, snagging on the memory of burning lungs and vanishing air.

His wife experiences him as both present and unreachable. He spends more time sitting silently in the yard at night, where he says the air feels cleaner. He startles if she approaches him from behind. Their grandchildren are told not to spray deodorant or insect repellent around him because he becomes visibly tense, his jaw set, eyes narrowed, as if preparing for impact. He hates that they notice. He has always been proud of being the calm center of the family, the grandfather who fixes things, the man who never flinches. Now he avoids family gatherings where there will be smoke from cooking fires, solvents, or crowded rooms with unfamiliar smells. He tells people he is tired, though what he means is that vigilance exhausts him.

He also carries anger that surprises him. He snaps over small household mistakes-an uncapped bottle of bleach, a leaking gas burner, a misplaced rag with paint thinner on it. Afterwards he feels guilty and retreats further. Sleep is poor. Some nights he dreams he is sealed inside his bomb suit, clawing at the visor as vapor curls in around him. Other nights he does not dream but wakes already braced, as if the alarm has been sounding for hours inside his body. In the morning, he stands at the sink longer than necessary, watching his own face and wondering how a man trained for visible threats is undone by something he cannot see.

What troubles him most in the present is not only fear but the collapse of certainty. He still goes to work, still dresses with care, still speaks in the measured tone of a technician who wants facts before conclusions. But beneath that discipline, his world has become organized around anticipation of contamination. He enters rooms and first notices the smell. He plans exits. He studies the air. Part of him knows he survived that day. Another part remains there, in the instant after the hiss, waiting for the invisible danger to reach him again.
